No later discovery obliged Emma to revise her unfavourable judgment of Mrs. Elton. Her perceptions had been sufficiently accurate. As the lady struck her at this second meeting, so she continued to strike her at every subsequent one: conceited, presumptuous, overfamiliar, uninformed, and wanting in breeding. She possessed a little prettiness and a few accomplishments, but so small a share of judgment that she imagined herself bringing superior worldly knowledge to enliven and refine a rural neighbourhood. She believed, too, that Miss Hawkins had enjoyed a standing in society which only Mrs. Elton's importance could exceed.

Nothing suggested that Mr. Elton's opinion differed from his wife's. He appeared not simply content with her, but proud of her. His manner conveyed self-congratulation at having introduced to Highbury a woman beyond even Miss Woodhouse's equal. Most of her new acquaintances were perfectly satisfied: whether inclined to praise, unaccustomed to forming judgments, guided by Miss Bates's benevolence, or simply assuming the bride as clever and agreeable as she declared herself. Thus Mrs. Elton's commendations circulated from mouth to mouth as they properly should, meeting no resistance from Miss Woodhouse, who willingly repeated her earliest contribution and spoke graciously of the lady as ‘very agreeable and most elegantly dressed.’

In one particular, Mrs. Elton became worse even than her first appearance had promised. Her disposition toward Emma changed. Probably wounded by the scant encouragement her overtures of intimacy received, she retreated herself, growing by degrees considerably cooler and more reserved. Although the consequence was welcome, the resentment producing it inevitably strengthened Emma's aversion. Both her behaviour and her husband's toward Harriet were disagreeable; they treated her with neglect and derision. Emma hoped this must soon cure Harriet's attachment, but the feelings capable of inspiring such conduct lowered them both greatly in her esteem. Doubtless poor Harriet's affection had been sacrificed to marital frankness, and Emma's own part in the affair had very likely been related as well, with every circumstance arranged to discredit her and comfort him. She was naturally an object of dislike to them both. Whenever other subjects failed, disparaging Miss Woodhouse must provide an easy conversation; and the hostility they dared not display in direct disrespect toward her found freer expression in their contempt for Harriet.

Mrs. Elton formed a strong liking for Jane Fairfax, and had done so from the outset. It was not merely after hostilities with one young lady might have made another seem desirable; it began immediately. Nor would she rest content with the expression of a natural, reasonable admiration. Unasked, without justification or entitlement, she must insist upon assisting and befriending her. Before Emma had lost her place as confidante, at approximately their third encounter, she heard the whole of Mrs. Elton's chivalrous schemes on Jane's behalf.

Having driven a peg with the utmost precision into the very place where the beetle had dropped, my friend took a measuring tape from his pocket. He secured one end to the part of the tree trunk closest to the peg, drew the tape out to meet it, and continued another fifty feet along the line defined by tree and peg, while Jupiter used the scythe to cut away the brambles. At the point thus reached he planted a second peg, around which he traced a rough circle some four feet across. Legrand then took a spade, handed another to Jupiter and a third to me, and urged us to begin digging without delay.

In truth, such recreation had never held much attraction for me, and at that particular time I should have been most willing to refuse it. Night was approaching, and our previous exertions had left me weary. Yet I could discover no means of escape and feared that a refusal would upset my unfortunate friend's composure. Had I been certain of Jupiter's assistance, I would unhesitatingly have tried to convey the madman home by force. But I knew the old black man's character too well to imagine that any circumstances would induce him to help me in a physical struggle with his master. I felt sure Legrand had succumbed to one of the countless Southern superstitions concerning buried money, and that the discovery of the scarab, or perhaps Jupiter's stubborn claim that it was ‘a beetle of solid gold,’ had strengthened his delusion. A mind inclined toward madness could easily be carried away by such hints, especially when they accorded with cherished notions already present. I remembered, too, the poor man's statement that the beetle was ‘the pointer to his fortune.’ Altogether, I was deeply troubled and perplexed. At last, however, I resolved to turn necessity into a virtue, dig willingly, and thereby show the dreamer with his own eyes, as soon as possible, how mistaken his beliefs were.

Once the lanterns were lighted, we set to work with an enthusiasm deserving of a more sensible undertaking. As their glare illuminated our bodies and tools, I could not avoid reflecting upon the picturesque group we formed, and upon how odd and suspicious our occupation would seem to any stranger who happened upon us.

For two hours we dug without slackening.

At the sight, Jupiter could hardly contain his delight, while his master's face expressed the keenest disappointment. Nevertheless, he pressed us to persist, and scarcely had he spoken when my boot caught in a heavy iron ring half concealed beneath the loose soil, sending me stumbling forward onto the ground.

Now we laboured in earnest, and no ten minutes of my life ever passed in greater excitement. Within that time we fully exposed an oblong wooden chest. Its extraordinary hardness and flawless preservation made it evident that it had undergone some mineral treatment, perhaps with bichloride of mercury. The box measured three and a half feet in length, three in width, and two and a half in depth. Riveted bands of wrought iron bound it securely, forming a sort of open lattice across its surface. Near the top on either side were three iron rings, six altogether, allowing six men to take a firm grip. Even our greatest combined effort scarcely shifted the coffer from its resting-place. We immediately recognized that moving such a weight was impossible. Fortunately, only two sliding bolts held the lid shut. Panting and trembling with eagerness, we pushed them back. A moment later, wealth beyond calculation shone before us. The lantern beams striking into the hole drew such a blaze of light from the jumbled mass of gold and jewels that our eyes were utterly dazzled.

I will not attempt to convey the emotions with which I stared. Wonder naturally surpassed them all. Legrand seemed drained by excitement and said almost nothing. For several minutes Jupiter's face took on as deathly a pallor as a black man's complexion could display. He appeared stunned, as though struck by thunder. Then he dropped to his knees inside the pit, plunged his bare arms elbow-deep into the gold, and kept them there as if savouring a luxurious bath. At last he released a profound sigh and exclaimed, seemingly to himself:

‘And all dis come from de gold-bug! De pretty gold-bug! De poor little gold-bug I treated so savage! Ain't you ashamed of yourself, nigger? Answer me dat!’

Eventually I had to awaken both master and servant to the need to carry away the treasure. The hour was growing late, and we must exert ourselves if everything was to be safely indoors before dawn. Deciding how to proceed was difficult. Our thoughts were all so disordered that we spent a considerable time discussing the matter.
